figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SleepXA. a. Conventional sleep FMs are pretrained on polysomnography (PSG) from scratch. b. Independently pretrained, open-sourced EEG and ECG FMs can be composed for sleep representation learning. c. SleepXA aligns common representations, preserves modality-specific information, and reduces redundancy between modalities. d. Representative evaluation spans sleep and non-sleep tasks (normalized by panel, higher is better; details in Section 4.2).

Figure 2: Sleep-guided cross-modality common-specific learning in SleepXA. a. Commonspace alignment combines instance- and stage-level alignment with distribution structural alignment within each cohort. b. Specific preservation matches each feature to its corresponding same-stagemodality prototypes while matching prototypes to their corresponding centroids. c. Disentanglement reduces redundancy between the two components while retaining complementary physiology.
Table 1: Sleep staging on three representative cohorts. Acc and MF1 are percentages; all metrics are higher-is-better. Bold and underlined values indicate the best and second-best results.

Figure 4: Age and sex prediction. Performance of foundation models under LP and FT. Age prediction is evaluated by MAE and RMSE (↓), while sex prediction is evaluated by Macro-F1 and AUROC (↑). Dashed lines denote the best supervised baselines.

Figure 5: Cross-context physiological transfer beyond nocturnal sleep. Performance across eight downstream settings involving EEG, ECG, EOG, and surface EMG. Foundation models are evaluated under LP and FT, and dashed lines denote the best supervised baseline for each setting.
Figure 8: Comparison of multimodal integration strategies. WSC sleep staging under (a) Full, (b) Core, and (c) EEG-only inputs, and (d) CinC2017 AF recognition under LP and FT.

Figure 9: Ablation of the major alignment objectives. Effects of removing CA, SP, or CD on (a) WSC sleep staging, (b) WSC OSA severity classification, and (c) CinC2017 AF recognition. Annotations report the change relative to the original SleepXA model under the same LP/FT setting.
Table A.1: Dataset configuration for alignment pre-training and downstream evaluation. Task IDs correspond to Table A.2.
Table A.2: Overview of the 27 downstream tasks. Task IDs correspond to those used in the cross-task performance summary.
Table A.3: Pre-training provenance of inherited EEG and ECG foundation encoders. LaBraM and CSFM have no cohort overlap with our downstream evaluation datasets.

Table A.5: Age prediction and sex classification on Test SHHS1/2. Lower values are better for MAE and RMSE, while higher values are better for R2, Acc, MF1, and AUROC. Bold and underlined values indicate the best and second-best model results.

Figure A.1: UMAP visualization of sleep-stage representations. Epoch-level representations from Test SHHS1/2, APPLES, and WSC are shown under LP (top) and FT (bottom). Points are colored according to the five sleep stages: Wake, N1, N2, N3, and REM.

Figure A.2: Illustrative whole-night predictions on a randomly selected WSC test recording. Recording ID: 39201. Panels show sleep staging under (a) LP and (b) FT, and respiratory-event detection under (c) LP and (d) FT. Prediction probabilities are shown with the corresponding groundtruth labels. Unevaluated epochs are removed and the remaining epochs are sequentially reindexed.

Table A.6: Sleep staging on small cohorts under subject-level five-fold cross-validation. Acc. and MF1 are percentages; all metrics are higher-is-better. Bold and underlined values indicate the best and second-best results.

Table A.8: Sleep spindle detection on MASS-SS2 using C3 EEG. E1 and E2 denote the two expert annotations. Bold and underlined values indicate the best and second-best results across all methods in each column, respectively, based on unrounded scores. Higher is better for all metrics.

Table A.7: Respiratory event detection performance on three representative cohorts. Acc. is reported in percentage, while AUPRC and AUROC are reported on a 0–1 scale. Higher is better for all metrics.
Table A.9: Performance comparison on AHI estimation and OSA severity classification across two representative cohorts.

Figure A.3: Detailed analysis of AHI estimation and OSA severity prediction. Results are shown for Test SHHS1/2 and WSC under linear probing (LP) and full fine-tuning (FT). (a) Four-level OSA severity confusion matrices for normal, mild, moderate, and severe OSA; (b) predicted versus reference AHI with regression statistics; (c) Bland–Altman agreement analysis between predicted and reference AHI; and d) subgroup performance across sex, age, and BMI strata, with S-0 to S-3 denoting normal, mild, moderate, and severe OSA, respectively. The subgroup analysis is included as a robustness diagnostic to examine whether predictive performance is concentrated in particular demographic groups.
Table A.10: Linear-probing performance for current disease diagnosis.

Figure A.4: Sleep-disorder classification on the CAP Sleep Database. Subject-level binary classification of heterogeneous sleep disorders versus healthy controls under full PSG (a–b) and central EEG-only (c–d) configurations. Results are reported as mean and standard deviation across five subject-level folds.

Table A.12: Controlled initialization study on WSC sleep staging. All variants share the same architecture and training configuration, differing only in the initialization of the EEG and ECG encoders. All metrics except Cohen’s κ are reported in percentages. Bold and underlined values denote the best and second-best results within LP or FT, respectively.

Figure A.5: Class-wise analysis of foundation-model initialization on sleep staging. Rownormalized confusion matrices are shown for four initialization settings under linear probing (LP, top row) and full fine-tuning (FT, bottom row). Rows denote ground-truth stages and columns denote predicted stages. Each cell reports the percentage within the corresponding ground-truth class.

Table A.14: Robustness to different EEG and ECG foundation-model backbones on WSC sleep staging. ∆ denotes the improvement of pretrained initialization over Scratch; bold indicates the best result within each setting.

Table A.15: Comparison of integration strategies across input configurations on WSC sleep staging. Bold and underlined values denote the best and second-best results within each configuration and adaptation setting.
Table A.16: Cross-context transfer on CinC2017 AF task. Results are reported as percentages. Best and second-best results are shown in bold and underlined, respectively.
Table A.18: Ablation of major objectives on WSC AHI estimation and OSA severity classification. Best results within each adaptation setting are shown in bold.

Table A.19: Ablation of major objectives on CinC2017 AF recognition. Ch-F1 and AF-F1 denote the F1 scores for the challenge metric and atrial fibrillation class, respectively. Best results within each adaptation setting are shown in bold.

Table A.20: Effect of sleep-stage labels on WSC sleep staging. MF1 denotes Macro-F1. Best results within each adaptation setting are shown in bold. Hybrid and partial variants retain expert SHHS labels.

Table A.21: Effect of sleep-stage labels on WSC AHI estimation and OSA severity classification. Acc. and MF1 evaluate OSA severity classification. Best results within each adaptation setting are shown in bold.
Table A.22: Effect of sleep-stage labels on CinC2017 AF recognition. All scores, including AFAUROC, are reported as percentages. Best results within each adaptation setting are shown in bold.

Figure A.6: Robustness to restricted modality availability. WSC sleep staging under LP with progressively reduced physiological inputs, from the full seven-modality PSG configuration to EEGonly evaluation.

Figure A.7: Effect of pre-training diversity and scale under limited downstream supervision LP performance using 5%, 10%, 25%, 50%, and 100% of the labeled downstream training subjects under single-domain, matched multi-domain, and full multi-domain pre-training. (a) WSC sleep staging, evaluated by Macro-F1; (b) WSC AHI estimation, evaluated by MAE; (c) WSC OSA severity classification, evaluated by Macro-F1; and (d) SEED-VIG vigilance estimation, evaluated by Pearson’s r.
